questions.stem:
A 27-year-old man comes to an STI clinic with 5 days of two painful, ragged ulcers on the shaft of the penis with a purulent base. There is a tender, fluctuant left inguinal lymph node. He had unprotected intercourse during a recent trip. Darkfield microscopy and syphilis serology are negative, and an HSV nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) of the ulcer exudate is negative.

Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?
choices: Treponema pallidum
Haemophilus ducreyi
Klebsiella granulomatis
Chlamydia trachomatis serovar L2
Herpes simplex virus type 2

explain.html: Genital ulcer diseases are sorted by two questions: is the ulcer painful, and what do the regional lymph nodes look like. Chancroid gives one or more painful ulcers with tender, suppurative inguinal adenopathy, while syphilis typically gives a single painless chancre, granuloma inguinale gives painless ulcers without adenopathy, and LGV gives a small self-limited lesion followed by adenopathy or proctocolitis. Chancroid is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi, a fastidious gram-negative facultative anaerobe that needs special culture media with sensitivity under 80%, and no NAAT is FDA approved. Diagnosis is therefore probable when painful ulcers are present and syphilis (darkfield and serology) and HSV (NAAT or culture) are excluded. This man has painful ragged ulcers, a fluctuant tender node, and negative syphilis and HSV testing, which meets those criteria. Treatment options are azithromycin, ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin or erythromycin, and partners from the 10 days before symptoms are examined and treated even if asymptomatic.
explain.table:
DiseaseOrganismUlcerNodes
ChancroidHaemophilus ducreyiPainfulTender, suppurative
Primary syphilisTreponema pallidumUsually single chancreRegional, within 7 days
Granuloma inguinaleKlebsiella granulomatisPainless, bleeds easilyNone (pseudobuboes possible)
LGVC. trachomatis L1 to L3Small, self-limitedUnilateral inguinal or femoral
Genital herpesHSV-1, HSV-2Recurrent lesionsVariable
why: Syphilis was excluded by negative darkfield and serology.
Granuloma inguinale produces painless ulcers without regional adenopathy.
LGV usually has only a small self-limited lesion, with adenopathy or proctocolitis dominating.
HSV was excluded by a negative NAAT of the ulcer exudate.
explain.takeaway: Chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi) is a probable diagnosis when painful genital ulcers with tender suppurative inguinal adenopathy occur and syphilis and HSV testing are negative.

explain.objective: Diseases characterized by genital, anal, or perianal ulcers

questions.stem:
A 35-year-old man who recently returned from 6 months working in India has a slowly enlarging, painless, beefy-red ulcer on the perineum that bleeds easily on contact. There is no inguinal lymphadenopathy, though there is a firm subcutaneous swelling near the groin. Cultures are unrevealing. A crush preparation of tissue from the ulcer edge shows dark-staining intracellular bacteria within mononuclear cells.

Which of the following best describes the required treatment course?
choices: A single intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G given today
Seven days of oral metronidazole
Topical imiquimod applied until clearance
One to five days of oral valacyclovir
At least 3 weeks of an oral antibiotic such as azithromycin

explain.html: Granuloma inguinale, or donovanosis, is caused by Klebsiella granulomatis, an intracellular gram-negative bacterium endemic in tropical and developing areas such as India, South America and South Africa. It produces painless, slowly progressive genital or perineal ulcers without regional adenopathy; the lesions are highly vascular and bleed easily. Subcutaneous granulomas called pseudobuboes can mimic nodes, and the infection can extend to the pelvis, abdomen, bones or mouth. The organism is difficult to culture, so diagnosis is made by seeing Donovan bodies on a tissue crush prep or biopsy. This man who worked in India has a painless beefy ulcer that bleeds on contact, no lymphadenopathy, a groin pseudobubo and intracellular bacteria on crush prep. Treatment must last at least 3 weeks with azithromycin, doxycycline, ciprofloxacin, erythromycin or TMP-SMX DS, and an aminoglycoside may need to be added.
explain.table:
InfectionTreatment length
Granuloma inguinaleAt least 3 weeks
LGV21 days
First-episode genital herpes7 to 10 days
Recurrent genital herpes1 to 5 days
Primary, secondary, early latent syphilisBenzathine penicillin G IM once
why: A single benzathine penicillin dose treats early syphilis, not donovanosis.
Metronidazole treats trichomoniasis and bacterial vaginosis.
Imiquimod is a topical treatment for anogenital warts.
Short valacyclovir courses treat recurrent genital herpes.
explain.takeaway: Granuloma inguinale (Klebsiella granulomatis) causes painless, easily bleeding genital ulcers without adenopathy, is diagnosed by Donovan bodies on crush prep and requires at least 3 weeks of antibiotics.

explain.objective: Diseases characterized by genital, anal, or perianal ulcers

questions.stem:
A 26-year-old man presents with 1 week of fever, malaise and a nonpruritic rash of copper-colored macules over the trunk, palms and soles. He has patchy hair loss, painless white mucosal patches in the mouth, and moist, flat, gray plaques in the perianal area. He has generalized lymphadenopathy. Two months ago he had a painless penile sore that healed on its own.

Which of the following is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis?
choices: A nontreponemal test with a treponemal test
Culture of the organism on artificial media
A nontreponemal test result alone
Gram stain of the perianal lesion
Viral culture of the oral lesions

explain.html: Syphilis, caused by Treponema pallidum, moves through stages: a primary chancre about 3 weeks after infection that heals on its own, then secondary syphilis, the disseminated and most florid stage, with fever, rash, generalized lymphadenopathy, mucosal lesions, alopecia, and sometimes nephritis or hepatitis. Moist flat perianal plaques in this stage are condylomata lata. This man's healed painless sore two months ago followed by fever, a palm and sole rash, patchy alopecia, oral mucosal patches, condylomata lata and generalized nodes is secondary syphilis. T. pallidum is a stealth organism that cannot be cultured on artificial media, so the diagnosis rests on serology. Serology uses a nontreponemal test (RPR or VDRL) and a treponemal test (FTA-ABS or TP-PA), and using only one is insufficient. The traditional algorithm starts with the nontreponemal test and the reverse-sequence algorithm with the treponemal test.
why: T. pallidum cannot be grown on artificial media; it can only be propagated in organ culture.
A single test type is insufficient to make the diagnosis of syphilis.
Lesions are examined by darkfield microscopy or immunofluorescent staining, not Gram stain.
Syphilis is a bacterial spirochete infection, not a viral one.
explain.takeaway: Secondary syphilis (palm and sole rash, condylomata lata, alopecia, mucosal lesions, generalized lymphadenopathy) is confirmed with both a nontreponemal and a treponemal test, because T. pallidum cannot be cultured.

rows.if_right: an organism that grows on standard laboratory media

rows.if_right: a screening step that will be followed by a confirmatory treponemal test

rows.if_right: a gram-negative organism such as gonorrhea

rows.why: Syphilis is a bacterial spirochete infection, not a viral one.
rows.if_right: painful oral or genital vesicles from HSV

questions.stem:
A 44-year-old man has 1 week of blurred vision and floaters in both eyes. Eye examination shows panuveitis. He has a faint rash on his palms. RPR is reactive at 1:128 and the treponemal test is reactive. He has no penicillin allergy.

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
choices: Benzathine penicillin G intramuscularly once
Benzathine penicillin G intramuscularly once weekly for a total of 3 weeks
Ceftriaxone intramuscularly once
Doxycycline orally for 14 days
Aqueous crystalline penicillin G intravenously for 10 to 14 days

explain.html: Syphilis treatment is chosen by stage and by whether the nervous system, eye or ear is involved. Primary, secondary and early latent syphilis get a single IM dose of benzathine penicillin G; late latent, unknown-duration latent and tertiary syphilis with negative CSF get benzathine penicillin weekly for 3 weeks. Ocular syphilis and otosyphilis can occur at any stage, usually early, and may or may not come with other CNS involvement; ocular disease is often panuveitis and can cause permanent vision loss. Neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis and otosyphilis are treated with aqueous crystalline penicillin G IV for 10 to 14 days. This man has panuveitis with a palm rash and an RPR of 1:128, which is ocular syphilis. Because ocular syphilis is managed in the same group as neurosyphilis, he needs the IV regimen rather than any benzathine schedule.
explain.table:
StageTreatmentAlternative
Primary, secondary, early latentBenzathine penicillin G IM onceDoxycycline 14 days
Late latent, unknown duration, tertiary (CSF negative)Benzathine penicillin G IM weekly for 3 weeksDoxycycline 28 days
Neurosyphilis, ocular, otosyphilisAqueous crystalline penicillin G IV for 10 to 14 daysNone listed
PregnancyPenicillin only, desensitize if allergicNone
why: A single IM dose treats primary, secondary and early latent syphilis, not ocular disease.
Three weekly IM doses treat late latent or tertiary syphilis without CNS disease.
Single-dose ceftriaxone is a gonorrhea regimen.
Doxycycline for 14 days is the alternative for early syphilis, not ocular syphilis.
explain.takeaway: Neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis and otosyphilis are treated with IV aqueous crystalline penicillin G for 10 to 14 days.

rows.if_right: secondary syphilis with a normal eye and neurologic exam

questions.stem:
A 25-year-old woman at 14 weeks of gestation has a reactive RPR at 1:16 and a reactive treponemal test at her first prenatal visit. She has a faint rash on the palms. She reports hives and wheezing after amoxicillin as a child.

Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
choices: Desensitize, then give benzathine penicillin G
Azithromycin as a single dose
Doxycycline for 14 days
Ceftriaxone for 10 days
Defer treatment until after delivery, then give penicillin

explain.html: Syphilis in pregnancy matters because T. pallidum can be transmitted vertically to the fetus, even from latent disease. Pregnant women are tested at the first prenatal visit and at week 28, and at delivery if they come from a community with high syphilis incidence; any woman with fetal death after 20 weeks is tested. In pregnancy the rule is only penicillin, and a patient with a penicillin allergy is desensitized rather than switched to another drug. For primary and secondary syphilis in pregnancy, an additional IM dose is given one week later. This woman at 14 weeks has a palm rash and reactive serology, which is secondary syphilis, and a history of hives and wheezing after amoxicillin. She should be desensitized and then treated with benzathine penicillin G, without delay.
why: Azithromycin is not among the listed syphilis regimens.
Doxycycline is a nonpregnant alternative; in pregnancy only penicillin is used.
Ceftriaxone is not the regimen for syphilis in pregnancy.
Deferring treatment risks vertical transmission to the fetus.
explain.takeaway: Syphilis in pregnancy is treated only with penicillin, and penicillin-allergic patients are desensitized first.
explain.subject: Microbiology

rows.why: Azithromycin is not among the listed syphilis regimens.
rows.if_right: a chancroid or chlamydia infection

rows.why: Doxycycline is a nonpregnant alternative; in pregnancy only penicillin is used.
rows.if_right: early syphilis in a nonpregnant patient with penicillin allergy

rows.why: Ceftriaxone is not the regimen for syphilis in pregnancy.
rows.if_right: gonorrhea in pregnancy

rows.why: Deferring treatment risks vertical transmission to the fetus.
rows.if_right: a patient who is not pregnant and is being scheduled for routine treatment

questions.stem:
A 29-year-old man reports 3 days of sore throat after receptive oral sex with a partner who was recently diagnosed with gonorrhea. A pharyngeal NAAT is positive for N. gonorrhoeae, and a urine NAAT is negative for both gonorrhea and chlamydia. He has no drug allergies.

Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?
choices: Doxycycline alone for 7 days
Ceftriaxone, with no further testing needed
Azithromycin plus gentamicin, then no follow-up
Ceftriaxone, with a test of cure afterward
Penicillin G benzathine as a single dose

explain.html: Uncomplicated gonorrhea of the cervix, urethra, rectum or pharynx is treated with ceftriaxone. Doxycycline is added only if chlamydia has not been excluded (azithromycin in pregnancy), and patients with an IgE-mediated penicillin or a cephalosporin allergy get azithromycin plus gentamicin instead. Whether to check a test of cure depends on the site. It is not necessary for uncomplicated urogenital or rectal gonorrhea treated with the recommended regimen, but it is recommended for pharyngeal gonorrhea regardless of the regimen. This man has a positive pharyngeal NAAT, a negative urine chlamydia test and no allergies. He gets ceftriaxone alone, followed by a test of cure because the infection is in the pharynx.
why: Doxycycline covers chlamydia, not gonorrhea.
Skipping the test of cure applies to urogenital and rectal infection, not pharyngeal.
Azithromycin plus gentamicin is reserved for IgE-mediated penicillin or cephalosporin allergy, and pharyngeal infection still needs a test of cure.
Benzathine penicillin treats syphilis, not gonorrhea.
explain.takeaway: Gonorrhea is treated with ceftriaxone, with doxycycline added when chlamydia is not excluded, and pharyngeal infection requires a test of cure.
explain.topic: Gonorrhea treatment and test of cure
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Diseases characterized by urethritis and cervicitis

rows.if_right: chlamydia alone, or chlamydia not excluded alongside ceftriaxone

rows.why: Skipping the test of cure applies to urogenital and rectal infection, not pharyngeal.
rows.if_right: uncomplicated gonococcal urethritis treated with ceftriaxone

rows.why: Azithromycin plus gentamicin is reserved for IgE-mediated penicillin or cephalosporin allergy, and pharyngeal infection still needs a test of cure.
rows.if_right: gonorrhea in a patient with a cephalosporin allergy

rows.if_right: primary or secondary syphilis

questions.stem:
A 27-year-old woman has 2 weeks of thin, grayish-white vaginal discharge with a fishy odor that is worse after intercourse. There is no itching or dysuria. Speculum exam shows a homogeneous discharge coating the vaginal walls and a normal-appearing cervix. Vaginal pH is 5.5. Adding potassium hydroxide to the discharge intensifies the odor, and a wet mount shows epithelial cells studded with bacteria and no motile organisms.

Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis?
choices: Invasion of the endocervical columnar epithelium by an obligate intracellular bacterium
Latent virus reactivating in sacral ganglia
Infection of squamous cells by a flagellated protozoan
Overgrowth of a gram-negative diplococcus in the vagina
Replacement of hydrogen peroxide-producing lactobacilli with anaerobes

explain.html: Bacterial vaginosis is a polymicrobial syndrome, not a single infection: the normal hydrogen peroxide-producing Lactobacillus species are replaced by anaerobic organisms. It is diagnosed by Gram stain or wet mount, or clinically when at least three of four criteria are met: a homogeneous, thin, white discharge coating the vaginal walls, clue cells, pH above 4.5 and a fishy odor on the whiff test. Trichomoniasis, by contrast, shows motile protozoa, and cervicitis shows endocervical exudate or bleeding. This woman has a thin homogeneous discharge, pH 5.5, a positive whiff test with potassium hydroxide and epithelial cells studded with bacteria, with no motile organisms and a normal cervix. She meets all four criteria for BV. Treatment is oral metronidazole, intravaginal metronidazole gel or intravaginal clindamycin cream.
explain.table:
FeatureBacterial vaginosisTrichomoniasis
CauseLactobacilli replaced by anaerobesProtozoan Trichomonas vaginalis
DischargeThin, homogeneous, fishy odorCopious, foul-smelling
Wet mountClue cellsMotile trophozoites
CervixNormalStrawberry cervix
TreatmentMetronidazole or clindamycin creamMetronidazole or tinidazole, treat partner
why: Endocervical infection by an obligate intracellular bacterium describes chlamydial cervicitis.
Latent virus reactivating in ganglia describes genital herpes, which causes lesions rather than this discharge.
A flagellated protozoan would be seen moving on wet mount in trichomoniasis.
A gram-negative diplococcus describes gonorrhea, which causes cervicitis rather than BV.
explain.takeaway: Bacterial vaginosis is replacement of hydrogen peroxide-producing lactobacilli by anaerobes, diagnosed by thin discharge, clue cells, pH above 4.5 and a positive whiff test, and treated with metronidazole or clindamycin.

explain.objective: Diseases characterized by vulvovaginal itching, burning, irritation, odor, or discharge

questions.stem:
A 30-year-old woman has a week of copious, frothy, foul-smelling yellow-green vaginal discharge with vulvar itching. Speculum exam shows punctate hemorrhages on the cervix. A wet mount of the discharge shows motile, pear-shaped organisms. She has one male partner who has no symptoms.

Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
choices: Metronidazole for her alone, since her partner has no symptoms
Ceftriaxone and doxycycline for both partners
Intravaginal clindamycin cream for her alone
Metronidazole for her and treatment of her partner
Fluconazole for her and her partner

explain.html: Trichomonas vaginalis is a protozoan with a motile trophozoite, and it causes a spectrum of disease in both sexes. In women it ranges from asymptomatic to copious, foul-smelling discharge with a strawberry cervix, and in men it ranges from asymptomatic to urethritis. Diagnosis is by wet mount, which shows the motile organisms, or by NAAT. This woman has foul frothy discharge, punctate cervical hemorrhages and motile pear-shaped organisms on wet mount, which is trichomoniasis. Treatment is metronidazole or tinidazole, and the partner must be treated. Her partner's lack of symptoms does not mean he is uninfected, since men are often asymptomatic, and untreated partners lead to reinfection.
why: Men are often asymptomatic, so the partner must be treated as well.
Ceftriaxone and doxycycline cover gonorrhea and chlamydia, not a protozoan.
Clindamycin cream treats bacterial vaginosis and does not treat Trichomonas.
Fluconazole is an antifungal, and Trichomonas is a protozoan treated with metronidazole in both partners.
explain.takeaway: Trichomonas vaginalis (motile trophozoites on wet mount, strawberry cervix) is treated with metronidazole or tinidazole, and the sexual partner must also be treated.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Diseases characterized by vulvovaginal itching, burning, irritation, odor, or discharge

questions.stem:
A 19-year-old man has several soft, flesh-colored, cauliflower-like papules on the penile shaft that are not painful. He has never been vaccinated against human papillomavirus. He asks whether vaccination would still help and what it protects against.

Which statement best matches this lesion and the nine-valent vaccine?
choices: Lesions are from types 16 and 18; the vaccine is only for those over 26
Lesions are from types 31 and 33; the vaccine is a single lifelong dose
Lesions are from types 16 and 18; the vaccine is approved only for women
Lesions are from types 6 and 11; the vaccine treats existing warts
Lesions are from types 6 and 11; the vaccine is recommended through age 26

explain.html: There are over 100 HPV types and more than 40 infect the genital area; most infections are self-limited and unrecognized. The types split into two groups. Non-oncogenic types, mostly 6 and 11, cause condyloma acuminatum, while oncogenic types such as 16 and 18 cause cervical, penile, vulvar, vaginal and oropharyngeal cancers and precancers. Warts are treated with imiquimod, podophyllin, trichloroacetic acid, cryotherapy or surgery. Gardasil 9 covers types 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58, is recommended at age 11 to 12 (starting as early as 9) and for all adults through age 26, given as a two- or three-dose series, and is FDA approved in both sexes through age 45 with shared decision making from 27 to 45. This 19-year-old unvaccinated man has cauliflower-like papules from types 6 and 11, and vaccination is still recommended for him to prevent infection with the other covered types, though it does not treat the existing warts.
explain.table:
HPV typesDiseaseIn Gardasil 9
6, 11Condyloma acuminatum (non-oncogenic)Yes
16, 18Cervical, penile, vulvar, vaginal, oropharyngeal cancerYes
31, 33, 45, 52, 58OncogenicYes
why: Types 16 and 18 are oncogenic, and the vaccine is recommended through age 26, not only after it.
Types 31 and 33 are oncogenic types in the vaccine, and the series is two or three doses.
Types 16 and 18 are oncogenic, and the vaccine is approved for both women and men.
The vaccine prevents infection and does not treat existing warts.
explain.takeaway: Genital warts come from HPV 6 and 11 while 16 and 18 are oncogenic, and Gardasil 9 is recommended for everyone through age 26 to prevent, not treat, infection.

questions.stem:
A 28-year-old man has persistent dysuria and mucoid urethral discharge 3 weeks after a course of doxycycline for nongonococcal urethritis. Gonorrhea, chlamydia and Trichomonas NAATs are negative. A NAAT is positive for a very small, slow-growing bacterium, and resistance testing shows a mutation conferring macrolide resistance.

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
choices: Doxycycline, then azithromycin
Doxycycline, then moxifloxacin
A cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone
Metronidazole or tinidazole
Benzathine penicillin G

explain.html: Urethritis is divided into gonococcal and non-gonococcal causes, and non-gonococcal urethritis comes from C. trachomatis, T. vaginalis or Mycoplasma genitalium, with no pathogen found in about half. M. genitalium is a tiny, slow-growing bacterium without a cell wall, so cell-wall drugs such as beta-lactams cannot work, and it is diagnosed by NAAT. Its treatment depends on macrolide susceptibility. Macrolide-susceptible strains get doxycycline followed by azithromycin, while macrolide-resistant strains, or cases without resistance testing, get doxycycline followed by moxifloxacin. This man has persistent urethritis after doxycycline, negative gonorrhea, chlamydia and Trichomonas tests, a positive NAAT for a tiny slow-growing bacterium and a macrolide resistance mutation. He therefore needs doxycycline then moxifloxacin.
explain.table:
M. genitalium strainTreatment
Macrolide susceptibleDoxycycline, then azithromycin
Macrolide resistant or not testedDoxycycline, then moxifloxacin
why: Azithromycin follows doxycycline only for macrolide-susceptible strains.
Without a cell wall, the organism is unaffected by cephalosporins.
Metronidazole and tinidazole treat Trichomonas, which tested negative.
Penicillin acts on the cell wall and treats syphilis, not M. genitalium.
explain.takeaway: Mycoplasma genitalium lacks a cell wall and is treated with doxycycline then azithromycin if macrolide susceptible, or doxycycline then moxifloxacin if macrolide resistant or untested.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Diseases characterized by urethritis and cervicitis

questions.stem:
A 52-year-old woman has a reactive RPR at 1:8 and a reactive TP-PA on routine testing before surgery. She has no symptoms, and examination including a neurologic and eye exam is normal. She has no prior syphilis tests on record and cannot recall any genital sore or rash.

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
choices: Benzathine penicillin G intramuscularly weekly for 3 weeks
Benzathine penicillin G intramuscularly once
Aqueous crystalline penicillin G intravenously for 14 days
No treatment, since latent syphilis is not transmitted sexually
Doxycycline for 14 days

explain.html: Latent syphilis is seroreactivity without signs or symptoms. It is early latent if infection occurred within 1 year and late latent if longer, and when the timing cannot be established it is called latent syphilis of unknown duration and managed as late latent. Latent syphilis is not transmitted sexually but is still treated to prevent complications, and it can be passed vertically to a fetus. Late latent, unknown-duration latent and tertiary syphilis with negative CSF are treated with benzathine penicillin G IM weekly for 3 weeks, with 28 days of doxycycline as the alternative. This woman has a reactive RPR and TP-PA, normal neurologic and eye exams, no prior tests and no memory of a sore or rash, so the duration is unknown. She gets three weekly doses of benzathine penicillin.
why: A single dose is for primary, secondary or early latent syphilis.
IV aqueous penicillin is for neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis or otosyphilis.
Latent syphilis is treated to prevent late complications even though it is not sexually transmitted.
Fourteen days of doxycycline is the early syphilis alternative; late latent disease needs 28 days.
explain.takeaway: Latent syphilis of unknown duration is managed as late latent and treated with benzathine penicillin G weekly for 3 weeks.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 31-year-old man who has receptive anal intercourse with men presents with 2 weeks of rectal pain, tenesmus and bloody mucopurulent discharge. Anoscopy shows proctitis. He recalls a small painless sore that healed on its own a month ago. A nucleic acid amplification test of the rectal swab is positive for an obligate intracellular organism that is also the most common bacterial cause of cervicitis in young women.

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
choices: Doxycycline for 7 days
Benzathine penicillin weekly for 3 weeks
Ceftriaxone as a single dose
Doxycycline for 21 days
Acyclovir for 7 to 10 days

explain.html: Lymphogranuloma venereum is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2 and L3, the invasive strains rather than those causing ordinary urethritis and cervicitis. It may begin with a self-limited papule or ulcer, followed by usually unilateral inguinal or femoral adenopathy. After rectal exposure, proctocolitis is the most common presentation. Definitive diagnosis needs LGV-specific molecular testing, which is not widely available, so diagnosis rests on clinical suspicion, epidemiology and a C. trachomatis NAAT at the symptomatic site; serology is not used. This man with receptive anal intercourse, proctitis after a healed painless sore and a positive rectal chlamydia NAAT fits LGV. The key management point is duration: LGV is treated for 21 days, with doxycycline, erythromycin or azithromycin, and retested 3 months after treatment.
why: A short doxycycline course treats uncomplicated chlamydia, not LGV.
Weekly benzathine penicillin for 3 weeks treats late latent or tertiary syphilis.
Single-dose ceftriaxone treats uncomplicated gonorrhea, not chlamydia.
Acyclovir treats HSV, a virus.
explain.takeaway: Lymphogranuloma venereum (C. trachomatis L1 to L3) commonly presents as proctocolitis after rectal exposure and is treated for 21 days, typically with doxycycline.

questions.stem:
A 40-year-old woman has routine STI screening. Her laboratory uses the reverse-sequence algorithm. She has no symptoms and no lesions on examination, and she does not recall ever being treated for syphilis.

[[labs 0]]

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
choices: Treat now with benzathine penicillin for latent syphilis
Report a false-positive result and stop
Repeat the RPR in 12 months
Perform a second, different treponemal test
Perform a lumbar puncture for CSF VDRL

explain.html: Syphilis serology pairs two test types. Nontreponemal tests (RPR, VDRL) measure antibody to a cardiolipin antigen and their titers track disease activity, while treponemal tests (FTA-ABS, TP-PA, immunoassays) measure antibody to T. pallidum antigens and usually stay positive for life. The traditional algorithm starts with a nontreponemal test; the reverse-sequence algorithm starts with a treponemal test and, if reactive, follows with a nontreponemal test. When the treponemal test is reactive but the nontreponemal test is nonreactive, the results are discordant, and the next step is a second, different treponemal test. A nonreactive second test suggests a biologic false-positive treponemal result, while a reactive one suggests treated syphilis, long-standing untreated syphilis or very early primary infection. This woman has exactly that discordant pattern with no history of treatment, so the second treponemal test decides what happens next.

Discordant results cannot be called false positive until a second treponemal test is nonreactive.
Waiting a year leaves a possible untreated infection unresolved.
She has no neurologic, ocular or otic findings that would call for CSF testing.
explain.takeaway: In reverse-sequence syphilis screening, a reactive treponemal test with a nonreactive RPR is resolved by a second, different treponemal test.

questions.stem:
A 33-year-old man was treated for primary syphilis with a single intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G. His RPR was 1:32 at diagnosis. He returns for follow-up.

[[labs 0]]

He reports a new painless genital ulcer.

Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation and plan?
choices: Serofast state; no action is needed
Expected lifelong positivity of a treponemal test
Possible failure or reinfection; retest HIV, consider LP, retreat
Biologic false positive; confirm the result with a treponemal antibody test
Adequate response; repeat the titer at 24 months

explain.html: After syphilis treatment, response is followed with the nontreponemal titer, because its titer correlates with disease activity and is reported quantitatively, such as 1:16. The goal is a 4-fold (two-dilution) decline, checked at 6 and 12 months for primary and secondary syphilis and at 6, 12 and 24 months for latent disease. Treponemal tests are not used this way, since they usually stay positive for life. Possible failure is defined by persistent or recurring signs or symptoms, or a 4-fold or greater rise in titer. This man's RPR fell appropriately from 1:32 to 1:4 by 6 months, then rose to 1:64 with a new painless ulcer, a 16-fold rise that marks possible treatment failure or reinfection. The plan is to repeat HIV testing, consider a lumbar puncture and retreat.
why: A serofast titer stays low and stable; it does not rise 16-fold with a new lesion.
Lifelong positivity describes treponemal tests, not the RPR.
He has proven, treated syphilis, so this is not a biologic false positive.
A rising titer with a new lesion is not an adequate response.
explain.takeaway: Nontreponemal titers track syphilis activity; a 4-fold rise after treatment signals possible failure or reinfection and calls for repeat HIV testing, consideration of LP and retreatment.
explain.subject: Microbiology

rows.if_right: a titer that fell and then stayed at the same low level without symptoms

rows.why: Lifelong positivity describes treponemal tests, not the RPR.
rows.if_right: a reactive FTA-ABS or TP-PA years after successful treatment

rows.why: He has proven, treated syphilis, so this is not a biologic false positive.
rows.if_right: a reactive RPR with a nonreactive treponemal test

rows.why: A rising titer with a new lesion is not an adequate response.
rows.if_right: a sustained 4-fold decline with no new signs

questions.stem:
A 22-year-old woman presents with 3 days of fever and pain in the right wrist and left ankle. Examination shows tenderness and swelling along the extensor tendon sheaths of the right hand and a few small pustules on a red base over the forearms. She has a new sexual partner and has had no genital symptoms. Synovial fluid is inflammatory, and a NAAT from the cervix is positive.

Which of the following best describes the causative organism?
choices: Gram-negative diplococcus
Spirochete seen on darkfield
Obligate intracellular coccoid bacterium
Bacterium lacking a cell wall
Motile flagellated protozoan

explain.html: The bacteria behind urethritis and cervicitis are told apart partly by their structure. Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a nonmotile, non-spore-forming gram-negative diplococcus; C. trachomatis is an obligate intracellular organism, Mycoplasma genitalium lacks a cell wall and Trichomonas vaginalis is a motile protozoan. Gonorrhea causes urethritis and cervicitis, and women are more often asymptomatic than men. It can disseminate, causing petechial or pustular skin lesions, asymmetric polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis and oligoarticular septic arthritis. This young woman with fever, tenosynovitis of the wrist extensors, asymmetric joint pain, pustules on the forearms and a positive cervical NAAT has disseminated gonococcal infection, even without genital symptoms. Diagnosis is by NAAT at urogenital and extragenital sites or by culture.
explain.table:
OrganismStructure
Neisseria gonorrhoeaeGram-negative diplococcus, nonmotile
Chlamydia trachomatisObligate intracellular, nonmotile
Mycoplasma genitaliumTiny, slow growing, no cell wall
Treponema pallidumCoiled spirochete, seen on darkfield
Trichomonas vaginalisMotile protozoan
why: A spirochete seen on darkfield describes T. pallidum.
An obligate intracellular organism describes C. trachomatis.
A bacterium without a cell wall describes Mycoplasma genitalium.
A motile flagellated protozoan describes Trichomonas vaginalis.
explain.takeaway: Disseminated gonococcal infection (tenosynovitis, asymmetric polyarthralgia, pustular skin lesions) is caused by the gram-negative diplococcus N. gonorrhoeae, often without genital symptoms in women.

questions.stem:
A 34-year-old man has 3 days of right-sided scrotal pain. Examination shows a swollen, tender right epididymis and a tender spermatic cord; the testis lies normally and the cremasteric reflex is present. Urinalysis shows pyuria. He has sex with men and reports insertive anal intercourse without condoms. Urethral NAAT results are pending.

Which empiric regimen best covers the likely organisms?
choices: Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline for 10 days
Levofloxacin alone for 10 days
Ceftriaxone plus levofloxacin for 10 days
Metronidazole for 7 days
Benzathine penicillin G as a single intramuscular dose

explain.html: Epididymitis presents with unilateral testicular pain and tenderness, swelling of the epididymis, a tender swollen spermatic cord and sometimes a hydrocele. Its causes are N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis and enteric organisms, and treatment is chosen by the likely cause. When gonorrhea and chlamydia are suspected, the regimen is ceftriaxone plus doxycycline for 10 days; when enteric Enterobacteriaceae are suspected, it is levofloxacin for 10 days. In men who practice insertive anal intercourse, both gonorrhea and enteric organisms are possible, so the regimen is ceftriaxone plus levofloxacin for 10 days. This man has a tender swollen epididymis and cord with a normal testis and reports insertive anal intercourse without condoms. He needs coverage for both gonorrhea and enteric gram-negative rods while his NAAT results are pending.
explain.table:
Likely causeRegimen (10 days)
Gonorrhea and chlamydiaCeftriaxone plus doxycycline
Enteric organisms (Enterobacteriaceae)Levofloxacin
Insertive anal intercourseCeftriaxone plus levofloxacin
why: Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline covers gonorrhea and chlamydia but not enteric organisms.
Levofloxacin alone covers enteric organisms but leaves gonorrhea uncovered.
Metronidazole treats Trichomonas and bacterial vaginosis, not epididymitis.
Benzathine penicillin treats syphilis.
explain.takeaway: Epididymitis is treated by likely cause: ceftriaxone plus doxycycline for gonorrhea and chlamydia, levofloxacin for enteric organisms, and ceftriaxone plus levofloxacin after insertive anal intercourse.

questions.stem:
A 29-year-old man comes to the STI clinic because a partner he had condomless sex with 3 weeks ago was just diagnosed with secondary syphilis. Four years ago he was treated for primary syphilis with benzathine penicillin G; his RPR fell from 1:32 to 1:2 and has stayed at 1:2 on every check since. He has no genital ulcer, rash, or lymphadenopathy, and neurologic and eye examinations are normal. His HIV test is negative.

[[labs 0]]

Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
choices: Aqueous crystalline penicillin G intravenously for 10 to 14 days
Repeat the RPR in 3 months and treat if it rises fourfold
No treatment, since his RPR titer has not risen
Benzathine penicillin G intramuscularly weekly for 3 weeks
Benzathine penicillin G intramuscularly once

explain.html:
Syphilis serology uses two kinds of tests. Nontreponemal tests (RPR, VDRL) measure antibody to a cardiolipin-lecithin-cholesterol antigen, and their titers track disease activity; after treatment the goal is a fourfold decline. Treponemal tests (FTA-ABS, TP-PA) measure antibody to T. pallidum antigens and usually stay positive for life. Median incubation is about 3 weeks, and a previously infected person may not develop a chancre, so a very recent infection can be present with no lesion and no serologic change. For that reason, a contact of early syphilis within 90 days is treated as early syphilis even if testing is negative.

His partner has secondary syphilis, an early stage, and the exposure was 3 weeks ago. His reactive FTA-ABS and stable RPR of 1:2 are the expected residue of his treated infection, so they neither prove latent disease nor exclude a new one. He receives the early syphilis regimen, benzathine penicillin G intramuscularly once, which treats an incubating infection before he can transmit it.
explain.table:
TestWhat it measuresAfter successful treatment
Nontreponemal (RPR, VDRL)Antibody to cardiolipin-lecithin-cholesterol; titer tracks activityFalls fourfold or more; may stay low and stable
Treponemal (FTA-ABS, TP-PA)Antibody to T. pallidum antigensUsually stays reactive for life
why: Aqueous crystalline penicillin is for neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis, or otosyphilis, and his examinations are normal.
Watching for a fourfold rise is how follow-up detects failure or reinfection, but it leaves a possible incubating infection untreated.
A titer that has not moved yet cannot exclude an infection acquired 3 weeks ago, so the 90-day rule calls for treatment.
Weekly dosing treats late latent or unknown-duration syphilis, and his treponemal reactivity comes from his documented treated infection.
explain.takeaway: Sexual contacts of early syphilis within 90 days receive one IM dose of benzathine penicillin G even if tests are negative; treponemal tests stay positive for life after treatment.

questions.stem:
A 24-year-old man has 10 days of dysuria and a scant mucoid urethral discharge. A week ago an urgent care clinic gave him a single injection of ceftriaxone and no other antibiotic, and his symptoms are unchanged. He has had no new partners since then. Gram stain of the discharge shows many neutrophils and no gram-negative diplococci. He took azithromycin for bronchitis last year.

[[labs 0]]

Which property of the causative organism best explains why the urgent care treatment had no effect?
choices: It lacks a cell wall, the structure ceftriaxone acts on
It has acquired a mutation conferring macrolide resistance
It produces a beta-lactamase that inactivates ceftriaxone
It lives only inside host cells, beyond reach of the drug
It is a motile protozoan rather than a bacterium

explain.html:
Urethritis is split into gonococcal and nongonococcal (NGU); NGU is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, Trichomonas vaginalis, and Mycoplasma genitalium, with no pathogen found in about half. Each organism has a defining feature that predicts which drug works: N. gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative diplococcus treated with ceftriaxone, Chlamydia is obligate intracellular, Trichomonas is a motile protozoan treated with metronidazole, and M. genitalium is a tiny, slow-growing bacterium without a cell wall. Ceftriaxone is a beta-lactam that acts on cell wall synthesis, so it cannot treat an organism that has no wall.

Here the Gram stain shows neutrophils without gram-negative diplococci, the gonorrhea, chlamydia and Trichomonas NAATs are negative, and the M. genitalium NAAT is positive. He received ceftriaxone alone, so the failure comes from a missing drug target, not from macrolide resistance, which would matter only for azithromycin. He needs doxycycline followed by azithromycin, or by moxifloxacin if the organism is macrolide resistant or untested.
explain.table:
Urethritis organismDefining featureTreatment
N. gonorrhoeaeGram-negative diplococcusCeftriaxone
C. trachomatisObligate intracellularDoxycycline
M. genitaliumTiny, slow growing, no cell wallDoxycycline, then azithromycin (or moxifloxacin if macrolide resistant)
T. vaginalisMotile protozoanMetronidazole or tinidazole
why: Macrolide resistance affects azithromycin, and he received ceftriaxone, not a macrolide.
An organism with no cell wall offers ceftriaxone no target, so enzymatic inactivation is not the explanation.
Obligate intracellular growth describes Chlamydia, whose NAAT is negative here.
A motile protozoan describes Trichomonas, whose NAAT is negative; M. genitalium is a bacterium.
explain.takeaway: Mycoplasma genitalium has no cell wall, so beta-lactams fail; treat with doxycycline then azithromycin, or doxycycline then moxifloxacin when macrolide resistant or untested.
